items.text: Execute instructions with cache reuse to produce a manifest plus content-addressed layers.

Push the manifest and missing blobs; sign, scan, and promote the digest CI tested.
Pull the image, create a writable layer, attach mounts and networks, apply controls, start the process.

variants.explanation: Inputs → build → registry → run. The same digest crosses environments; run-time inputs decide how each instance behaves.

variants.hint: Replacing the container is the deployment, not editing inside it.
variants.explanation: Test runtime policy by replacing the container, not by restarting the process inside it.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process
variants.context: The image is a versioned delivery artifact; the container is a replaceable process. Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer. Deploy by digest; a tag is only a reference. Containers share the host kernel.
variants.prompt: A database writes its authoritative files into the container’s writable layer. What happens when the container is replaced?
options: Nothing, because the writable layer is committed back.
Docker migrates the writable layer into the replacement container.
The data is lost; authoritative files belong in a named volume.
optionFeedback: Only the image layers persist; the writable layer is never committed back on its own.
Nothing migrates a writable layer, and the replacement starts again from the image.
The writable layer disappears with the container.
variants.explanation: Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process

variants.prompt: Production deploys myapp:latest. Why is that risky?
options: The latest tag is deprecated and will stop resolving.
A tag is a mutable reference; deploy the tested digest.
Tag lookups add a registry round trip on every pull.
optionFeedback: latest is only a naming convention, and nothing about it is being removed.
The tag can point at a different image tomorrow.
The extra lookup is trivial; the real risk is that the tag can move.
variants.explanation: An image is content-addressed; a tag is only a reference.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process
variants.context: The image is a versioned delivery artifact; the container is a replaceable process. Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer. Deploy by digest; a tag is only a reference. Containers share the host kernel.
options: Yes, each container boots its own small kernel.
Yes, the same isolation but with no hypervisor underneath.
No. Containers share the host kernel; a VM has its own.
optionFeedback: No kernel boots; the container is just a process on the host kernel.
The hypervisor is what supplies VM isolation, so removing it changes the boundary.
Kernel compatibility and host hardening stay part of the security model.
variants.explanation: Choose the boundary from the threat model, not from image size.

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: Every code change reinstalls all dependencies. What should change in the Dockerfile?
options: Build on a machine with more cores and faster disk.
Disable the layer cache so builds stay predictable.
Copy the manifests and install before copying source.
optionFeedback: More hardware reinstalls faster but still reinstalls on every code change.
Turning the cache off makes every build reinstall, which is the problem, not the fix.
Stable inputs before frequently changing ones keeps the install cached.
variants.explanation: Read the Dockerfile as a cache graph.

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: The build context is the whole repository, including gigabytes of test data. What helps?
options: Adding build stages so that each stage copies less data.
A .dockerignore that excludes generated and test files.
A smaller base image, which shrinks what must be uploaded.
optionFeedback: Stages split the build, but the whole context is still sent to the daemon first.
A narrow context uploads less and invalidates less.
The base image is pulled by the daemon and has nothing to do with context size.
variants.hint: What does the builder have to observe?

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: A registry token is passed with ARG during the build. Where can it end up?
options: In image metadata, a layer, the cache, or the build logs.
Nowhere, because ARG values are discarded after the build.
Only in the final image, which is scanned before release.
optionFeedback: Secret and SSH mounts expose credentials only to the instruction that needs them.
ARG values persist in image history and can be read back with docker history.
It also reaches the build cache and the CI logs, which scanning the image never sees.
variants.explanation: Keep credentials out of image history.

variants.prompt: A Dockerfile has six instructions. Instruction 3 changes. How many instructions must rerun?
variants.hint: The changed instruction and everything after it.
variants.explanation: Instructions 3, 4, 5, and 6 rerun; 1 and 2 stay cached.

mistakes.feedback: Dependent instructions after the change also rerun.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: Temporary scratch files that may disappear with the container. Where do they belong?
options: A named data volume.
A bind mount onto a host path.
The container writable layer.
optionFeedback: Volumes are for data with an independent lifecycle.
A bind mount exposes a host path, which outlives the container entirely.
Process-local, disposable changes fit the writable layer.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: Persistent application data must outlive containers. Which placement, and what does it not provide?
options: A tmpfs mount large enough to hold the whole dataset.
A named volume; it survives replacement but is not a backup.
The container writable layer, which survives a restart in place.
optionFeedback: tmpfs lives in memory and vanishes on restart, let alone on replacement.
Define ownership, backup, restore, migration, and deletion policy separately.
A restart may reuse the container, but a replacement discards the writable layer.
variants.hint: Does surviving replacement equal being backed up?
variants.explanation: A volume survives replacement; it does not automatically provide a backup.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: A container runs as root with the host Docker socket mounted. What is the risk?
options: Slower disk I/O, since every write must cross the socket.
It effectively has host-level privilege over the daemon.
None, since the container namespace still isolates it.
optionFeedback: The socket is a control channel, not a data path, so throughput is not the issue.
Runtime capabilities should be declared deliberately.
Containers share the kernel, and the socket lets the process start a privileged one.
variants.explanation: Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege explicitly.
